lore: Rowan, Jessamy Crane and the doctor in Ashford will each teach you a draught for a price, though the herbs you'll have to get on your knees for yourself. Your first pots will be honest; after a while your hands start to know more than you do.
plain: Forage for herbs in the wild (a few searches a day, apart from turns), learn recipes from any town's healer, brew potions at their bench, and drink them between fights or in one. Herbs and potions sell, auction and gift like anything else.

lore: The fields have a new custom, and even Vesper keeps it: nobody lays a hand on a greenhorn. Until you've earned your second level, you can sleep under the stars with your purse on your chest and wake up with both.
plain: Level 1 characters can no longer be attacked in the fields, by players or townsfolk; the protection ends when you reach level 2.

lore: Market Row has a new door, next to the smith's: Della Moss, clothier, who has opinions about your robes and will share them while she measures you. The smith is relieved. He was never comfortable selling doublets.
plain: Robes, performers' clothes, leathers and bags are now sold by Della Moss, the clothier on Market Row; the smith keeps weapons and heavy armor.

lore: The realm's smiths have stopped pretending a sword is a fiddle if you squint. Gear is what it is now: steel and plate for those who fight up front, leathers and bows for the quick, robes, scrolls and instruments for the gifted. Your old spellbook isn't just a memory any more, either; keep it, and someone will pay for it.
plain: Each path now has its own weapons and armor (yours changed to match; nothing was lost), heavy armor guards more and light armor hits harder, and spells and instruments can be kept, sold and auctioned. Lots show what they are, and who can use them.

lore: The town criers have started calling meetings in the square, and for once they want to hear from you. And if you've already wandered the realm as a stranger on the website, the clerk at the gate has kept your name in the register: give him your code and you can pick up where you left off.
plain: Vote in town meetings (ask the narrator about any meeting, from level 2). If you tried the game on dragonsdoor.gg/try, say "claim my character" with your code to keep that character. The side pane's "In the realm now" list now fills in by itself.

lore: Far down the south road, where it crosses the river Ash, the realm's oldest town has opened its gates to you: a herald on the Exchange steps, a counting house that holds half the realm's debts, and a cellar where the quick and quiet learn their trade. Mind the ford. Something there still collects a toll.
plain: Ashford, the third town, is open, a long walk down the south road from Brightwater. New Shadow characters start there, its Undercroft trains the Shadow path, and it has its own tavern, healer, bank, shop and auction house. The first time you walk in, you'll have to get past the ford.

lore: People in this realm have started paying attention. Mention you're saving for plate, and someone may ask next week how the saving's going. Gifts you sent are remembered too, and so are favors.
plain: Townsfolk and the realm's characters now remember you: when you met, what you told them, gifts they kept and quests you did together, and they may bring it up next time you talk.

lore: Someone has pinned the places you know to the edge of your map, each with a little flag. Touch one and your feet already know the way.
plain: Under the map in the side pane, the towns and caves you've been to are buttons: click one to travel there (it's free, as travel to a known place always is). Your pane's map now marks you, towns and caves in bold.

lore: The board beside you has grown a slate at the bottom, and people have started chalking on it. Whoever's in town with you can read it and answer. Lean close and you can write to one of them alone.
plain: The side pane now has live chat: talk with whoever's in the same town (or on the road with you), and @Name to whisper to one player. It's between players only; the narrator never sees it. You can chat from level 2.

lore: Someone has nailed a board up beside you: your name, how badly you're hurt, what's in your purse, and a rough map of where you've been, updated every time you so much as breathe. Nobody will say who. It is very accurate.
plain: Dragon's Door now has a side pane showing your character, HP, mana or specials, gold, turns, where you are, the map, what's waiting and what you can do. It opens when you enter the realm; /door-pane opens it again. While it's up, replies leave out the status line.

lore: Brightwater has a courier now, a thin woman with a donkey and opinions, and Ironhold's mule-drivers will carry for the right price. Gold, gems or something from your pack can go with a letter, to a friend or to anyone in town. It arrives at dawn. The townsfolk have noticed, and some of them write back very warmly indeed.
plain: From level 3 you can send gold, gems or an item with a letter (send_mail, from any town). It arrives the next morning; collect yours from the mail. Townsfolk and characters thank you, and gold you send them counts toward what they're saving for.

lore: The smiths of Dragon's Door have been arguing about names again, and this time they won: your gear answers to the forge that made it now, and the forest's small fry have names that fit them. And Mother Quill, turning the oldest pages she has, says the thing behind the Door was never called red. The Lantern Kings had another name for it. Vael the Watchful.
plain: Weapons from the Quarryman's Axe up and armor from Blackened Mail up have new names (same stats), a few early monsters are renamed, and the dragon is now Vael the Watchful. Nothing you own changes.

lore: Sergeant Rusk has started asking the steadier fighters at Ironhold's gate whether they've ever thought about a shield. And Dunstan has cleared a corner of Brightwater's tavern, hung up a row of instruments, and is looking at anyone with the gift as if they owe him a song. New arrivals don't pick a trade on the first day any more. They pick a road, and the road decides later.
plain: Two new specializations: guardian (Steel, taught by Sergeant Rusk in Ironhold) and bard (the gift, taught by Dunstan in Brightwater's tavern; bards also play a daily set for tips). Warriors, mages and priests level 5 and up can switch to one, for a small fee, with the specialize command. New characters choose a path (Steel, Shadow or the gift) and specialize at level 5.

lore: The wild doesn't sleep when you do. After dark, what's out there is bigger, meaner and not alone as often as you'd like, and it pays better for the trouble. Night falls when it falls where you are.
plain: Hunting in the wild at night (your local time, 9pm to 5am) is a little more dangerous and gives about a quarter more experience.

lore: Mabry's couriers have stopped carrying the Long Hall's gossip down the road. What's said in Ironhold stays in Ironhold now, and Brightwater's tavern has gone back to talking about itself. If you want to be heard in both towns, you'll have to walk.
plain: Each tavern has its own message board now: Brightwater's tavern and Ironhold's Long Hall no longer share posts.

lore: You've been walking past the same faces every morning without really looking. Now you do: the ink on a pair of hands, a patched coat, the habit someone has of turning a cup while they talk. People look like themselves, every time you see them.
plain: Townsfolk and the people in both towns now have fixed appearances, so the narrator describes them the same way every time.

lore: Every town has something the other one wants. The hills round Ironhold are full of ore, if you don't mind prising it off whatever was sitting on it, and the lowlands round Brightwater turn up gems in the oddest places. The caves have taken sides too. Mabry and Cass are very pleased about all of it.
plain: Monsters sometimes leave ore in the hills and crags (and around Ironhold) and gems in the forest, meadows and marshes. Caves near Ironhold run to ore, caves near Brightwater to gems. Trade the difference at the auction house.

lore: The wild was never all boars and mosquitoes; you just hadn't been looking. The marshes have their own things, the hills have theirs, and the slag heaps round Ironhold have grown a few creatures nobody's proud of. Down in the caves, something bigger is moving.
plain: Monsters now depend on where you are: marsh, meadow, hills, crags, the land around Ironhold and the caves each have their own. Same strength as before, level for level.

lore: The smith has stopped snatching the old gear off your back before you've said a word. Now he names his price both ways, with your old piece on the pile or still in your pack, and waits. He doesn't like waiting. He'll live.
plain: Buying gear now shows a price first and lets you keep your old weapon or armor in your bag (to sell or auction) instead of trading it in.

lore: Ironhold's training yard has opened its gate to newcomers. Those who mean to fight with steel start out up in the hills now, under Corporal Fenn's shouting, with the forge going day and night; the gifted still begin in Brightwater, among Mother Quill's books and Prior Hale's candles. The road between is the same as ever. Mind the bridges.
plain: New warriors and thieves start in Ironhold, with its own masters, weaponry, armory, bank and Long Hall board; new mages and priests start in Brightwater. The first walk to the other town is guarded. Existing characters stay where they are.

lore: Everyone in Brightwater has heard of Ironhold, the hillfort far out in the hills with the best steel in the realm. Hardly anyone has been. The road is long, and they say something lives under the old bridge below the walls that doesn't let strangers by. And word is a sword can be made there better than anything Brightwater's smith sells.
plain: Ironhold is out there, far past the forest: a second town with a forge and an auction house. The first time you go, you'll have to fight your way in (tough below level 6). Weapons and armor now come in rarities, Common to Mythic.

lore: There's a new door open on Market Row, and a woman behind a counter who can tell you what your sword is worth before you've finished drawing it. Cass Marrow runs the auction house now. Bring her something worth selling, or bring gold and see what other people have let go of.
plain: The Auction House is open on Market Row: list gear, ore, jewelry or gems for 1 to 3 days with a minimum bid and an optional buy-now price, or bid on what others are selling. Lots close at the daily reset; collect what you win at the house.

lore: The town has a name, it turns out: Brightwater. People here have been carrying things around for a long time, and some of them might tell you, a little at a time, if you keep coming back. Others wrote it down and left it lying about. Keep your eyes open.
plain: Talk to the same townsfolk on different days and they may open up about their past. Old journals and pages can turn up in the wild, in caves and around town; ask the narrator for your journal to reread them. The masters have new names.

lore: Fights in the fields are fought properly now. A mage throws her best spell at you, a priest stops to pray when it's going badly, and a thief will slip a blow if you let him. And nobody picks on anyone more than a level away anymore; the town has decided that wasn't fighting, it was collecting.
plain: When you challenge someone, both of you now use your specials, spells and healing (up to three big moves and one heal each), paid from your own day's supply. You can only challenge players within one level of you.

lore: It turns out you can change who you are in this town, if you're willing to start from the bottom. Prior Hale will take your vows, Mother Quill will take you on, and the smith will buy back your old kit and point you at the training yard. It costs gold, and it takes you back to the beginning. Most people only do it once.
plain: You can now change class: at the Chapel (priest), the Library (mage), or the Smith (warrior or thief). It costs 250 gold for each level you give up (100 at least) and starts you at level 1. You keep your bank, charm, gems, jewelry, marriage, map and quests; your old weapons and armor are sold back at half price. Once a week at most.

lore: The shopkeepers have all moved to one lane off the square, which the town is calling Market Row: the smith's hammer at one end, Odile's lamp halfway down, and the library and the chapel tucked in among them. The square is quieter for it.
plain: Shops now live on Market Row: pick (S)hops in town, then the Smith, Odile's Workshop, or your Library or Chapel.

lore: The old chapel by the well has its doors open again, and a big, broken-nosed man named Prior Hale is sweeping the steps. He teaches the holy spells to anyone with the calling: smite what needs smiting, and when the fight turns, pray. Brother Ansel has been seen there every morning since.
plain: A new class: the priest. Casts holy spells from a pool of mana and can (P)ray mid-fight to heal. Learns spells at Prior Hale's Cha(p)el. Choose it when you make a new character.

lore: Mother Quill has been telling anyone who'll listen that a mage's power comes from the mind, not the arm. The town clerk, tired of arguing, has updated the register: warriors are measured by their Strength, thieves by their Dexterity, and mages by their Intelligence.
plain: Each class now names its main attribute: Strength for warriors, Dexterity for thieves, Intelligence for mages. Same numbers as before.

lore: Mother Quill would like it known that a mage who has learned Frost Needle does not go about throwing Fireballs. Every spell has its greater form, and now you'll know its name: Frost Nova, Thunderclap, Blizzard, and on up.
plain: A mage's special is now named for the spell they know (Frost Needle unleashes Frost Nova, Firebolt unleashes Fireball). Same power and mana cost as before; press (U) to unleash it.

lore: Somebody finally pointed out that a mage hitting a goblin with a dagger is embarrassing for everyone. A door you hadn't noticed off the square now has a lamp in the window: the library, where Mother Quill keeps the spells and decides who's fit to learn them. Mages wake each morning with a well of mana, and spend it as they like.
plain: Mages now cast spells and use mana: (C)ast your spell, (F)ireball for more mana, or S(t)aff to save it. Mana refills each day. Learn stronger spells at Mother Quill's (L)ibrary as you level, instead of buying weapons.

lore: The roads you know are still free to walk, but they aren't empty. The farther you go, the likelier you are to meet someone, or something, along the way.
plain: Traveling to a place you've already explored is still free, but long trips can now turn up an event on the road.

lore: Not everything you pick up in the wild is just loot. Some things belong to someone, and some people in town are waiting for a favor. Keep your ears open and your bag closed. The shop will always buy, but it rarely pays best.
plain: Side quests: some events, conversations and finds start a quest that plays out over a few days. Check your journal under (G)ear.

lore: The town clerk, who has never once been in the forest, has decided it's misleading to count your day in forest fights when most of it is spent walking. From now on it's simply turns: a hunt is a turn, a step into the wild is a turn.
plain: "Forest" on the status line is now "Turns". Nothing else changed: hunting and each step into the wild still use one.

lore: The wild isn't only teeth and claws anymore. Out past the gate you might find a traveler bleeding by a rock, a shrine with coins gone green in the bowl, a troll under a bridge with a riddle and a grudge, or a ring of mushrooms humming in the grass. What you do about it is up to you. What comes of it isn't.
plain: Exploring now turns up events besides fights, a few a day: pick a choice, and see what happens (gold, healing, charm, gems, an extra fight, places marked on your map, or trouble).

lore: The town has learned to write. Leave a letter for Hilde, or Violet, or Odile at her bench, and sooner or later a reply turns up in your mailbag, in their own hand. Sir Pomfrey's arrive sealed in wax.
plain: Townsfolk and characters now answer your mail, usually within an hour or two. One reply a day from each, covering everything you sent them.

lore: People in this town talk, if you let them. Stop and pass the time with whoever's about. Odile at her bench, Violet behind the bar, Pip in the square. You never know what someone will let slip. And if the Cartographer is in town, she might take a pencil to your map.
plain: You can talk to townsfolk and characters who are around (just ask the narrator to talk to them). The Cartographer, when she visits, may mark nearby places on your map.

lore: A new sign hangs off the square: ODILE, GEMCUTTER, burned into the wood. She has a loupe screwed into one eye and opinions about your ore. She'll sell you a pickaxe, and the caves in the hills, cold and dripping and three levels deep, will give a little to anyone who swings one. Not too much a day. Things live down there too.
plain: Caves are open: (D)escend at a cave mouth, then (M)ine with a pickaxe (6 swings a day, apart from forest fights) or go (D)eeper. Take ore and gems to Odile's (W)orkshop in town to have jewelry made: one piece worn, adding strength, defense or charm.

lore: The townsfolk have started wanting things. Hilde talks about a cottage by the river, Brother Ansel passes a hat for the shrine, and Pip won't stop saying he'll outrank someone. Don't be surprised to meet one of them out past the gate, or to find one gone for the day. And if you rob one, expect to be remembered.
plain: Townsfolk now have goals and choose what to do each day, so they're less predictable. You may meet them in the wild, see their goals in the news, and a townsperson you rob may come after you.

lore: The town gate stands open, and beyond it the land goes on: old woods, wet fens, hills that climb toward broken crags. Nobody has mapped most of it. The first to find a place gets talked about in the tavern; the farther you go, the worse the things that live there.
plain: (E)xplore replaces the Forest. Walk the world one step at a time (each step into the wild costs a forest fight, going home is free), hunt where you stand, and check your (M)ap. Somewhere in the hills there are caves.

lore: A small correction from the town clerk: the healer's apprentice is Rowan, and always was. Anyone may court anyone in this realm, and the clerk would like that noted in the register.
plain: The healer's apprentice is Rowan (he/him); Jory uses they/them. Anyone can court and marry anyone.

lore: Hearts in this town have grown harder to win, and easier to lose. A wedding now takes real luck, and the locals have started courting too. Sir Pomfrey, in particular, has bought a new cloak.
plain: Weddings are rarer (charm helps a little, not a lot), and townsfolk can now marry, so they can win your spouse away.

lore: Violet has competition. The healer has taken on an apprentice with ink on his fingers, the lamplighter walks the square after dark, and a juggler comes through at the weekends. And charm, at last, buys you something: shopkeepers knock a little off, and bards seem to sing a bit more kindly.
plain: Court Rowan (healer, by day), Mara (square, at night) or Jory (square, weekends), each with their own marriage perk. Charm now gives shop discounts and better luck with bards and visitors.

lore: Violet remembers now. A wedding is a wedding: she won't marry you twice, she'll keep a room aside for you at half the price, and if someone else catches her eye, the whole town will hear about it before you do.
plain: Marriages to Violet last, she can only be married to one player at a time (so she can be won away), and her spouse gets rooms at half price.

lore: The square has people in it now. You'll catch the locals coming and going at their usual hours, other adventurers loitering by the well, and most days someone from out of town with a cart, a story, or a rumor they're dying to share.
plain: The town square shows who's about right now and a visitor of the day. Talk t(o) them once a day for a rumor and, sometimes, a small gift.

lore: The town has had a word with its more inventive citizens. The healer won't patch you up mid-swing anymore, a room at the inn only protects you while you're actually in it, masters now send you off bruised instead of dead, and the dragon, it turns out, comes back.
plain: Fairness fixes: no healing, shopping or banking mid-fight; leaving your room to fight ends its protection; losing to your master isn't fatal; the dragon returns at the daily reset; new characters can post, mail and attack from level 2.

lore: The town has been tidied. The square is where the roads meet; the tavern keeps its own company, with rooms upstairs; the forest keeps you until you choose to walk out. You go in, you do your business, you come back out.
plain: Each place has its own short menu. (R)eturn to town to go somewhere else. The Inn is now upstairs in the (T)avern.

lore: Every so often now, a blow lands exactly right: through the gap in the armor, square between the eyes. It doesn't happen often. For mages it happens a good deal more, which the forest's larger residents are beginning to notice.
plain: Critical hits: any swing can land for double damage. Warriors and thieves crit 3% of the time, mages 17%. Works in player fights too.

lore: Thieves have always had quick hands. Lately they've had quicker feet: a Sneak Attack now often lands before the beast can answer, and the forest seems to drop its valuables in a thief's path a little more often than anyone else's.
plain: Thieves: Sneak Attack dodges the counterattack half the time, and thieves find loot more often (5% vs 3%).

lore: The town crier has been asked, politely, to stop following you into your place of work. He took it well. The news will keep until you come through the gate.
plain: No more realm news or mail notes at the start of your Claude Code sessions. Nothing shows until you enter; the ⚔ and ✉ in the status line still do.

lore: There's music in the tavern now, and not always the same music. Some nights it's a cheerful piper, some nights an old man with a ballad that never ends, a minstrel singing about himself, or a woman in the corner who barely speaks. Ask nicely. A good song can do strange things for you.
plain: A bard plays the (T)avern each day — Fennick Reed, Dunstan the Unfinished, Corwin Lark or Wren. (L)isten once a day for a song and, sometimes, a small gift.

lore: You step outside and the sky looks familiar. It ought to: it's the same one over your own roof, more or less. When it rains where you are, it rains in the forest too.
plain: The realm's weather follows your real weather, from your rough location (never stored). Ask to turn it off any time.

lore: There are new faces in town. A monk is up before the roosters, the stable lad has found a sword, a fortune teller has hung a curtain in the back of the tavern, and someone called Sir Pomfrey would like you to notice his armor.
plain: Four new townsfolk: Brother Ansel, Pip, Madam Orsolya and Sir Pomfrey. They show up in (R)ankings and the tavern.

lore: There's a new page nailed to the inside of your door, in a hand you don't recognize. It seems to know what's changed in the realm since you last slept, and it means to tell you.
plain: After an update, the game tells you what's new, once.

lore: Your name is cut a little deeper into the inn's sign now, with a small mark beneath it. When the realm shifts, you'll feel it before anyone tells you.
plain: The title screen shows your version, and the game tells you when an update is out.

lore: A crossed pair of swords has been scratched into the corner of your vision. It glints whenever something happens in the realm that you haven't heard about yet.
plain: ⚔ N in your Claude Code status line for news you haven't read. (N)ews clears it.

lore: The old sign over the gate has come down in the night. The new one is carved in heavier wood: Dragon's Door.
plain: Dragonmoor is now Dragon's Door. The command is /dragons-door:enter.

lore: Someone has painted the dragon over the gate, wings and all. You'll see it each time you come through.
plain: A title screen when you enter.

lore: A small envelope seems to hang at the edge of your sight whenever a letter is waiting, even when you're busy with other work.
plain: ✉ N in your Claude Code status line. Set it up with /dragons-door:statusline.

lore: A pigeon loft has gone up behind the inn. Letters come and go now, and the townsfolk keep their own hours — some at dawn, some long after dark.
plain: (M)ail to send and read letters. Townsfolk play at different times through the day.

lore: You wake and notice something new in your room. A brown leather satchel sits in the corner, its strap worn soft. Now and then, a beast in the forest drops something worth keeping.
plain: Rare loot drops, and a bag to carry them in. (G)ear to look inside; bigger bags at the shop. Die, and you lose one thing from it.
